newsitem.title: FRANCE: Local investors soak up pressure on French bonds.
newsitem.headline: Local investors soak up pressure on French bonds.

text.p: The French ruling centre-right coalition may have ditched its leader and be heading towards election defeat but some things in France don't change: domestic investors keep buying bonds.

Hamstrung by restrictions on overseas investing, ambivalent about whether the left or right will win, hungry for yield and facing a flood of bond redemptions in the next three months, French investors step in whenever the bond market drops.
"When the U.S. opened on Monday afternoon and a skeleton outfit started selling, the phones just started ringing, investors are simply watching for the dip," a trader at a French bank in Paris said.

The same happened on Tuesday. Eager non-resident traders returned from a long weekend to take a crack at a French market on the defensive since the opposition left scored a surprise win in the first round of a parliamentary election.
But domestic investors once again snapped up bonds at the lows, keeping French 10-year government bond yields a comfortable 10 basis points lower than German 10-year yields.
"Domestics took advantage of the correction to buy paper throughout Monday and were there again on the buy side this morning at the lows," another trader said.

The 10-year spread snapped into minus three basis points in early trading on Monday from minus 14 before the first round election results but quickly returned to minus 10. On Tuesday it moved in again to minus eight but was soon back at minus 10.
French domestic investors hold nearly 90 percent of outstanding government debt, reducing the impact foreign sales can have in comparison to other European bond markets.

Steady demand for bonds in 1996, fuelled partly by shifts in domestic retail savings from short-term investment vehicles to longer-term higher-yielding instruments, confounded many analyst predictions that French 10-year yields would not fall below German yields.
Dominique Barbet, bond analyst at Banques Paribas, said domestic investors appeared unconcerned whether the left come to power or the centre-right coalition retained its majority.

"There's a high probability we will have a left government, but the conclusion investors draw is that whether it's the left or the right it won't put France's economic policies in question," Barbet said.
He said investors expected France to continue its current policy of trimming public deficits and to remain committed to the timetable for a single European currency.
Analysts said one factor behind the buying was that domestic investors were preparing for a flood of cash from bond redemptions by turning cash into bonds whenever yields rose.

According to Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais, the total amount of cash to be returned to investors from government bonds and domestic French franc bonds in the next three months amounts to 271.8 billion francs ($47.6 billion). The repayment of the so-called Balladur bond on July 16 will contribute 90 billion francs alone.
"They're expecting to receive large amounts of cash in the next three months...so its normal they're reducing levels of cash now," Barbet said.

A bond salesman at a French bank said while investors were buying bonds now, many were waiting on the sidelines until after the second round of voting on June 1 in the hope a left win would produce another setback, and more attractive yields.
"They don't believe the elections are very serious. They're buying in the 10-year area...but many are waiting for it to go lower," he said.
